newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco experts want urgent administration reform.
newsitem.headline: Morocco experts want urgent administration reform.

text.p: A group of Moroccan experts on Wednesday called for urgent reform of the country's administration and modernisation of its judiciary system to attract foreign investments.

At the opening ceremony of a three-day scientific meeting on "The place of Morocco in the World", the delegates said the meeting aimed at discussing the social and economic issues hampering its development.

The meeting, organised by the Ribat al-Fath association, was led by officials including advisers to the royal palace. It is expected to draw up recommendations to be published next year, an official said.

"Morocco has chosen the liberalisation option and linkage of its economy with the world free market...Therefore we have to upgrade our economy, including the administration and justice," Mustapha El-Alaoui, secretary-general of the tourism ministry, told the meeting.
El-Alaoui said the kingdom could not present an adequate picture of a modern and democratic state unless urgent measures were taken.
"If Morocco has no justice with international standards we cannot attract foreign investors and set up an environment of confidence abroad," El-Alaoui said.

Earlier this year the World Bank urged Morocco to modernise its judiciary system and reduce the number of civil servants -- estimated at 750,000, excluding the security and armed forces -- to guarantee balanced economic growth.

Wages in the public administration remained a burden for the state budget and were estimated at 18 billion dirhams ($2.04 billion) in 1996/97 or the equivalent of the investment budget, said Tawfik Mouline, head of forecasting at the finance ministry.

"The wage volume of the Moroccan administration represents 11 percent of Morocco Gross Domestic Product (GDP)...If reforms were taking place, we could save a lot of money but unfortunately the structural adjustment programme did not touch the bureaucrats," Mouline said.
Morocco ended its 10-year economic structural adjustment programme in 1992 but the administration and justice were not included, he added.
He said direct foreign investment remained low at an estimated two percent of Morocco's GDP in 1996 against three percent at the start of the 1990s.
According to the latest figure the country's GDP was $31.8 billion in 1995 and is expected to reach $37.9 billion by end 1996, officials said.

In a brief statement, Agriculture Minister Hassan Abou Ayoub told the meeting: "Without a reform of the administration and justice, Morocco cannot overcome the challenges of the economy liberalisation and competitiveness on the world market."
Morocco has gradually liberalised its market commodities and lifted tariff barriers to comply with the World Trade Organisation rules since May 1996.

"If we do not speed up our reforms, one third of our industrial units will disappear due to the aggressive competitiveness of foreign firms which will invade our market in 1997," a Moroccan expert added.
